extracted.intended_audience: British political class and educated public concerned with constitutional reform and the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the composition, restraints, and moral foundations of representative bodies and constitutions; criteria for who should govern and how property and authority should be protected in a modern state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of those vested with supreme authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the supreme authority is vested in a body so composed, it must evidently produce the consequences of supreme authority placed in the hands of men not taught habitually to respect themselves,--who had no previous fortune in character at stake,--who could not be expected to bear with moderation or to conduct with discretion a power which they themselves, more than any others, must be surprised to find in their hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid entrusting supreme power to men from humble or turbulent backgrounds who are unaccustomed to self-respect or public responsibility; such persons are likely to be intoxicated by sudden greatness, pursue private interests, join litigious constitutions, and unsettle property and institutions. Selection should favor those with tested character and a stake in public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of professional predominance (lawyers, doctors, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty of law... and the faculty of medicine... had not, any more than that of the law, possessed in France its just estimation. Its professors... are formed to be instruments, not controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow legislatures to be dominated by narrow professional habits (lawyers, physicians, stock-jobbers). Professional excellence in a trade does not necessarily qualify one for statesmanship; a chamber monopolized by such professions will be prone to chicane, short-sighted private interests, and incapacity for comprehensive governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for representation of landed interest and established distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is a due and adequate representation of a state, that does not represent its ability, as well as its property. The characteristic essence of property... is to be unequal. The great masses... must be put out of the possibility of danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A representative body should include the natural landed interest and large proprietors in significant weight to defend property and to serve as a 'natural rampart' for lesser properties. Unequal accumulation of property is natural and must be protected rather than diffused in ways that weaken defense against plunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of fundamental laws, conventions, and checks
rubrics_metrics.description: That assembly... has no fundamental law, no strict convention, no respected usage to restrain it. Instead of finding themselves obliged to conform to a fixed constitution, they have a power to make a constitution which shall conform to their designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions must include enduring restraints—fundamental laws, respected usages, and countervailing institutions (e.g., an upper chamber, royal prerogative of dissolution)—to prevent a single assembly from unbounded power and arbitrary remaking of the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification of those who make or remake constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: What ought to be the heads, the hearts, the dispositions, that are qualified, or that dare, not only to make laws under a fixed constitution, but at one heat to strike out a totally new constitution for a great kingdom...?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entrust constitutional framing to persons possessing comprehensive knowledge, experience in mixed affairs, prudence, and dignity; avoid empowering those lacking a connected view of internal and external interests to create wholesale constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative selection should favor tested merit over easy elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: The road to eminence and power, from obscure condition, ought not to be made too easy... If rare merit be the rarest of all rare things, it ought to pass through some sort of probation. The temple of honor ought to be seated on an eminence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices of high trust should require probation and difficulty to test virtue and talent; avoid mechanisms that make elevation commonplace or effortless (rotation, blind sortition) which do not select for capacity to meet responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of sortition/rotation as general methods for large-scale governance
rubrics_metrics.description: No rotation, no appointment by lot, no mode of election operating in the spirit of sortition or rotation, can be generally good in a government conversant in extensive objects; because they have no tendency... to select the man with a view to the duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on random selection or short rotations for bodies entrusted with complex, long-term, national governance; selection methods should seek to match individual capacities to the duties required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of protecting family transmission of property
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of perpetuating our property in our families is one of the most valuable and interesting circumstances belonging to it, and that which tends the most to the perpetuation of society itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and institutional arrangements that allow property transmission across generations are crucial for social stability; policy should recognize the role of hereditary property and distinction as incentives and guarantees that bind private interest to public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Peers and hereditary element as safeguard of property
rubrics_metrics.description: With us the House of Peers is formed upon this principle. It is wholly composed of hereditary property and hereditary distinction, and made, therefore, the third of the legislature, and, in the last event, the sole judge of all property in all its subdivisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An upper chamber grounded in hereditary property provides a check and final arbiter on property questions; such institutional design is defended as a means to secure property rights against temporary popular passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must reflect ability as well as numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is a due and adequate representation of a state, that does not represent its ability, as well as its property... ability is a vigorous and active principle, and as property is sluggish, inert, and timid, it never can be safe from the invasions of ability, unless it be, out of all proportion, predominant in the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical majority is not sufficient basis for legitimate governing authority; representation must ensure talent and capacity (ability) are strongly present to counterbalance property’s inertia and to govern effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of leveling and democratic absolutism
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who attempt to level never equalize. In all societies consisting of various descriptions of citizens, some description must be uppermost. The levellers, therefore, only change and pervert the natural order of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy aiming simply to level social distinctions will not create equality but will unbalance necessary social hierarchies; preserve sensible distinctions rather than pursuing abstract egalitarian leveling that undermines order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational suitability for public honor and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The occupation of a hair-dresser, or of a working tallow-chandler, cannot be a matter of honor to any person... Such descriptions of men ought not to suffer oppression from the state; but the state suffers oppression, if such as they... are permitted to rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While no honest occupation should be oppressed, not all occupations produce the dispositions suitable for governance; avoid granting unchecked ruling power to classes formed by servile or narrowly mercenary employments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of abstract 'rights of man' when forming civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Far am I from denying in theory, full as far is my heart from withholding in practice, the real rights of men. In denying their false claims of right, I do not mean to injure those which are real... If civil society be the offspring of convention, that convention must be its law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize real natural rights but reject sweeping abstract claims that ignore the conventions and limits necessary for civil society; rights must be reconciled with the institutional needs and conventions of political association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental rule: no man should be judge in his own cause
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the first motives to civil society, and which becomes one of its fundamental rules, is, that no man should be judge in his own cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A foundational principle of governance is impartial adjudication; institutional design must prevent personal adjudication of one's own interests and secure neutral processes of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against confounding legitimacy solely with popular representation
rubrics_metrics.description: They must therefore look on this gross and palpable defect of representation... as rendering our whole government absolutely illegitimate... Their principle... goes much further than to an alteration in the election of the House of Commons... If popular representation, or choice, is necessary to the legitimacy of all government, the House of Lords is, at one stroke, bastardized and corrupted in blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy cannot be reduced to mere form of popular choice; a constitution’s title rests on historical conventions, institutions, and continuity—so reforms must consider deeper sources of legitimacy beyond simple numerics of representation.
